title: The Citadel Project is a Thief-inspired dark fantasy, survival-horror lite stealth-em-up with some lovely shadows set in a medieval megastructure
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
Big building, quiet moves

You know, given the whole stealthy element of Thief-like immersive sims, I'm surprised there haven't been more of them with horror elements. There's Gloomwood, sure, but it's not as common as I'd like. That in turn then makes me curious about The Citadel Project, an immersive sim with some survival-horror elements set in a nasty, parasite-infected dark fantasy world, all apparently made by just one person.

In The Citadel Project, "the last line of defense built by the Ancient Kings in an attempt to preserve what remains of humanity in the face of the Great Storm." Some kind of evil force is ruining it from the inside, and you have to make your way through a medieval megastructure to figure out what happened. You aren't anyone special, "just a simple prisoner who manages to escape from a cell deep within the Citadel." Truthfully, the story sounds fine enough, I'm more smitten with the vibes put on display.

The shadows are what sells me, for the most part. They're dark and moody, looking plenty ripe for hiding in. And look, if you hand me a megastructure to explore, I'm going to do so. I'm also a fan of your main weapon, a crossbow. Not enough games with crossbows if you ask me! There's all sorts of bolts you can use with it, like a fire bolt that, obviously, sets things or enemies alight, a rope bolt to help you quickly climb or swing out of danger, a decoy bolt that makes a lot of sound to distract with, or a moss bolt; I'm not sure what that one does, my guess would be to dampen your footsteps and make it easier to sneak up on unsuspecting baddies.

Said baddies also appear to be infected with some kind of parasite, the severing of which appears to come in handy when trying to take them down. Overall, The Citadel Project likes a neat little im sim with just enough going on to make me curious to explore further. Which I might do, when I get the chance, as there is a demo available on Steam. Alternatively, I could just wait a week, as the game is out in early access November 11th, just over a week away. You can wishlist it on Steam right here.

title: 7,500 Light-Years From Earth, A Cat’s Head Appears - Nautilus
content:
Looking at the images NASA just published from its Hubble and James Webb Space telescopes, you’d think part of the Carina Nebula was haunted. The vast cloud of gas and dust in these images resembles a cat sitting upright, with an eerily glowing eye.

It’s called the Cat’s Head Nebula, a piece of the Carina Nebula that, while not newly discovered, has been newly zoomorphized and nicknamed. It’s around 7,500 light-years away from Earth, carved out over eons by intense ultraviolet radiation and winds from the massive stars that call this region of the universe home.

That distinctive eye is thought to be a newly forged star, still largely cloaked in the dust that makes up the pillar shape that stretches below. Different densities of material are eroded at different rates, which gives us spectacular shots like these.

The Hubble Space Telescope image is the one capturing visible light, with the yellow ridges around the cat evidence of gas being ionized and lit up by ultraviolet radiation. Astronomers think photoevaporation might be happening here, which happens when gas is heated to such an extent it effectively boils off and disperses. You can also see oxygen lit up in blue, hydrogen glowing green, and sulfur burning red.

The two James Webb Space Telescope images chronicle the same scene in near-infrared and mid-infrared wavelengths, light that you wouldn’t see if you were peering out of a passing spaceship at the nebula. Near-infrared reveals some of the starlight partially hidden by dust, which is why the body of the cat looks more transparent. We get a better view of the background, though the thickest of the orange dust filaments are still visible.

The mid-infrared image is more about heat than light, and it’s the ghostliest of the lot—it really does look like a spectral feline keeping watch in space. The white outlines are created by the warmth of the dust and other carbon-based molecules that make up the Cat’s Head Nebula.

As always with these shots, the colors are chosen at the image-processing stage; the telescopes are grabbing the light readings in black, white, and gray.

title: Trump vs. WSJ Libel Lawsuit over Trump's Alleged Birthday Wishes to Epstein Thrown out
content:
The Article

On July 15, 2025, Palazzolo emailed then White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt ("Leavitt") advising her that Dow Jones intended to publish an article (the "Article") about a birthday letter that President Trump purportedly created for Epstein (the "Letter"). President Trump and his team responded quickly. Leavitt called Palazzolo and told him that the "subject matter" of the proposed Article was false. President Trump, through counsel, denied writing the Letter and warned Dow Jones not to publish the story. {President Trump also denied writing the Letter in an interview before publication.} And President Trump directly told Murdoch that he had not signed or sent the Letter. When Murdoch responded that he would "handle it," President Trump thought the WSJ would not print the Article. Two days later, the WSJ online edition published the Article.

The title of the Article—"Jeffrey Epstein's Friends Sent Him Bawdy Letters for a 50th Birthday Album. One was from Donald Trump"—is in bold print, with a subtitle below reading "[t]he leather-bound book was compiled by Ghislaine Maxwell. The president says the letter 'is a fake thing.'" Leading with a picture of President Trump with Epstein, the Article states the following, in pertinent part:

It was Jeffrey Esptein's 50th birthday, and Ghislaine Maxwell was preparing a special gift to mark the occasion. She turned to Epstein's family and friends. One of them was Donald Trump.

Maxwell collected letters from Trump and dozens of Epstein's other associates for a 2003 birthday album, according to documents reviewed by The Wall Street Journal.

Pages from the leather-bound album—assembled before Epstein was first arrested in 2006—are among the documents examined by Justice Department officials who investigated Epstein and Maxwell years ago, according to people who have reviewed the pages. It's unclear if any of the pages are part of the Trump Administration's recent review….

The letter bearing Trump's name, which was reviewed by the Journal, is bawdy—like others in the album. It contains several lines of typewritten text framed by the outline of a naked woman, which appears to be hand-drawn with a heavy marker. A pair of small arcs denotes the woman's breasts, and the future president's signature is a squiggly "Donald" below her waist, mimicking pubic hair.

The letter concludes: "Happy Birthday—and may every day be another wonderful secret."

In an interview with the Journal on Tuesday evening, Trump denied writing the letter or drawing the picture. "This is not me. This is a fake thing. It's a fake Wall Street Journal story," he said.

"I never wrote a picture in my life. I don't draw pictures of women," he said. "It's not my language. It's not my words."

He told the Journal he was preparing to file a lawsuit if it published an article. "I'm gonna sue The Wall Street Journal just like I sued everyone else," he said….

Justice Department officials didn't respond to requests for comment or address questions about whether the Trump page and other pages of the birthday album were part of the agency's recent documents review. The FBI declined to comment….

Among those who submitted letters were billionaire Leslie Wexner and attorney Alan Dershowitz … Wexner declined to comment through a spokesman … Dershowitz, who represented Epstein after his first arrest, said, "It's been a long time and I don't recall the content of what I may have written….

The book was put together by a New York City bookbinder, Herbert Weitz, according to people who were involved in the process. Weitz, who died in 2020, listed Epstein as a client on his website in 2003.

It isn't clear how the letter with Trump's signature was prepared. Inside the outline of the naked woman was a typewritten note styled as an imaginary conversation between Trump and Epstein, written in the third person.

[Description of Conversation]

When he turned 50, Epstein was already wealthy from managing Wexner's fortune and was socializing with Trump, Clinton and other powerful people. He often entertained at this Manhattan townhouse, Palm Beach, Fla., home and private Caribbean island….

Epstein and Trump spent time together in the 1990s and early 2000s and were photographed at social events, including with Maxwell and Melania Trump….

Trump, along with others including Clinton, also appeared several times on flight logs for Epstein's private jet.

A 2002 New York magazine profile of Epstein quoted Trump. "I've known Jeff for 15 years. Terrific guy," Trump said. "He's a lot of fun to be with. It is even said that he likes beautiful women as much as I do, and many of them are on the younger side. No doubt about it—Jeffrey enjoys his social life."

Both men said that they subsequently had a falling-out. Trump has said their friendship ended before Epstein pleaded guilty to procuring a minor for prostitution in 2008, served time in a Florida jail and registered as a sex offender….

Maxwell, a British socialite, was convicted in 2021 of helping Epstein's sex-trafficking and sentenced to 20 years in prison. Maxwell didn't respond to a letter requesting an interview sent to her in prison. Arthur Aidala, an attorney who represented Maxwell, said, "At this point, she is focused on her case before the Supreme Court of the United States." …

Epstein's associations with Trump and many powerful people have been well documented….

On September 8, 2025, the WSJ published an article titled "A Visual Breakdown of the Trump Birthday Letter to Epstein" which compares the signature and typeface, drawing style, third-person point of view, and diction in the Letter with prior communications by President Trump (the "September 8 Article"). The September 8 Article includes President Trump's denial that he wrote the Letter or drew the picture and Leavitt's statement in a social media post that President Trump did not draw the picture in or sign the Letter….

President Trump contends that these statements are false because he (1) did not author, sign, or draw any portion of the Letter or direct anyone else to author it; (2) never made or dictated to anyone any of the statements in the voiceover or had any such conversation with Epstein as portrayed in the Letter; and (3) was not "childhood pals" with Epstein….

The court concluded that Trump hadn't actually alleged "actual malice," which is to say knowing or reckless falsehood:

Here, the Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice. Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false.

[a.] Conclusory Language is not Enough

As an initial matter, President Trump's conclusory allegations that Defendants acted with malice because they "knew or should have known" the statements in the Article were false, are insufficient to state a claim. See Reed v. Chamblee (11th Cir. 2025) (finding the plaintiff's conclusory assertions that the defendant acted with actual malice insufficient).

[b.] Denial is not Enough

Though vague, the Amended Complaint appears to allege that by choosing to publish the Article despite President Trump's and his team's denials, Defendants acted with actual malice. In effect, President Trump argues that once he declared the Letter a "fake," Defendants should have disregarded everything else they learned in their investigation and not published the story.

But that is not what the actual malice standard requires and runs afoul of the First Amendment. Indeed, were that the law, any time a public figure or his team denies an accusation, journalists would be immediately blocked from publishing negative or contradictory press—a result that flies in the face of the "American privilege to speak one's mind, although not always with perfect good taste, on all public institutions[.]" Sullivan.

Moreover, the Article did not ignore or minimize President Trump's denial. Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it. By "allowing readers to decide for themselves what to conclude from the [Article], … any allegation of actual malice [is] less plausible." … "[R]eporting perspectives contrary to the publisher's own should be interpreted as helping to rebut, not establish, the presence of actual malice" ….

[c.] The Investigation

President Trump's argument that the WSJ Defendants' investigation was inadequate, and therefore an indication of malice, fares no better. As detailed above, a failure to investigate, without more, does not establish actual malice. Rather, "a plaintiff must show the defendant deliberately avoided investigating the veracity of the statement in order to evade learning the truth."

The Amended Complaint comes nowhere close to this standard. Indeed, the Article details a thoughtful and detailed investigation. Before running the story, Defendants contacted President Trump and his team, Justice Department officials, and the FBI for comment.

President Trump and his team responded with his denial, the Justice Department did not respond at all, and the FBI declined to comment. Defendants also attempted to speak with Maxwell; she did not respond to their request and her attorney stated that she was focused on her case before the Supreme Court. In addition, Defendants reached out to other individuals named in the Birthday Book, including Leslie Wexner and Alan Dershowitz, and to individuals involved in binding the Birthday Book, who confirmed that Weitz put the book together. In short, President Trump's allegation that Defendants failed to conduct an adequate investigation is rebutted by the Article and is insufficient to establish actual malice.

{President Trump argues that Harte-Hanks Communications, Inc. v. Connaughton (1989), supports his position that Defendants' purported failure to investigate is enough to support an inference of actual malice. However, in Harte-Hanks, the Supreme Court expressly stated that "[a]lthough failure to investigate will not alone support a finding of actual malice, the purposeful avoidance of the truth is in a different category. Here, President Trump has not alleged any facts, beyond conclusory allegations, that support an inference that Defendants purposefully avoided the truth.}

Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation. First, it alleges that the investigation was lacking because Defendants only reviewed the Letter but did not have a copy in their possession. The Court cannot discern any substantive difference—and certainly not one that would establish actual malice—between Defendants reviewing the Letter before publication and obtaining a copy of the Letter. Defendants reviewed the Letter and later reported on its contents. Nothing in the law suggests that Defendants needed to obtain, retain, or publish a copy.

In addition, President Trump's focus on Maxwell is entirely misplaced. The Eleventh Circuit has found "allegations that the Defendants failed to fully investigate their statements by intentionally choosing not to speak with any witnesses who could have refuted the allegedly defamatory statements" insufficient to plead actual malice. And any argument that Defendants "purposely avoided" the truth by either not disclosing what Maxwell told them or by refusing to speak with her is difficult to reconcile with President Trump's own allegations.

The Amended Complaint alleges that "Maxwell has stated, subject to penalty of perjury for lying to a federal officer, that she did not remember President Trump submitting a letter for Epstein's 50th birthday." Based on this allegation, Maxwell had little to offer to Defendants' investigation. In short, references to Maxwell are a red herring and simply do not establish that Defendants "actually entertained serious doubts as to the veracity of the published account[] or was highly aware that the account was probably false."

[d.] Omissions

President Trump's argument that the Article omits certain facts does not save his claims. First, how or why the voiceover in the Letter was typewritten or how the voiceover was confirmed to be in the third person are inconsequential details that have no bearing on whether Defendants published the Article knowing its contents were false or with reckless disregard as to its falsity. Moreover, Defendants' decisions about how to investigate and what to include in the Article do not establish malice. "Obviously the author of an article will have to choose which facts to include and which to omit. It is impossible to print all of the facts on which an opinion or belief is based …. Were the courts or criticized [parties] to be allowed to dictate the contents of such articles, censorship would have won out over free speech and the right to dissent."

Finally, the allegation that Defendants intentionally omitted President Trump's denial that he signed the Letter or a discussion on whether the signature on the Letter is authentic, is belied by the Article. It states, multiple times, that President Trump denies writing the Letter and that "[i]t isn't clear how the letter with Trump's signature was prepared." . This is more than sufficient to encompass any denial that he "signed" the Letter or that the signature on the Letter is authentic.

[e.] The September 8 Article

The Amended Complaint's reliance on the September 8 Article to establish malice is equally unavailing. Nothing in the law suggests that a journalist must report on every piece of evidence they uncover before going to print. Moreover, it is unclear why President Trump argues the September 8 Article shows that his signature "could not be more different" than the one in the Letter, when it contains several examples where President Trump's actual signature and sketches are similar to those in the Letter. At bottom, the September 8 Article does not support a finding that Defendants knew or should have known that President Trump did not sign the Letter….

title: Oldest Evidence of Human Cannabis Use Has a Ghoulish Twist - Nautilus
content:
A group of horses is called a “herd,” unless they’ve been ritually sacrificed. Then they’re called a “spectral cavalcade.” The term comes from writings of the Greek historian Herodotus describing the funerary practice of the Scythians, a group of nomadic horseback riders that roamed the Central Asian steppes until around the third century BCE. 

Of course, not all of Herodotus’ records were accurate (he mentioned dog-sized ants that harvested gold, for example), but the spectral cavalcade turned out to be (literally) dead on. Archaeologists discovered burial mounds in southern Siberia topped with the cadavers of sacrificed horses. Now, beneath the spectral cavalcade, they’ve discovered something else Herodotus was right about: The Scythians used cannabis as part of their funeral rites.

Read more: “What Goes on in the Brain When a Good Buzz Gets Harshed”

A team of researchers led by anthropologists from the Max Planck Institute analyzed remains discovered at the Tunnug 1 site, a Scythian burial mound in Siberia’s Uyuk Valley dated to around the first decade of the 8th century BCE. The team found more than 1,400 cannabis seeds strewn about the interiors of deteriorating log coffins. According to the team, the small size of the seeds indicates they likely came from wild plants and not cultivars.

They also found human hair—including a strikingly preserved braid—that they essentially drug tested. Every single sample tested contained low levels of THC and relatively higher levels of cannabinol, a product of THC breakdown. Prior to this find, the oldest evidence of cannabis use came from residue from 2,500-year-old Chinese braziers. Not only does this discovery push the earliest known cannabis use back three centuries, it’s also the first case where both the plant product and its biomolecular traces were discovered in the same archaeological context.

“These data add to the growing global repertoire of archaeological evidence for ancient people using plants as mind-altering or mood-altering drugs,” the researchers wrote in a study published today in Science. “Early cannabis use thus emerges not simply as a pharmacological curiosity but as an indication of how ancient societies experimented with and ritualized the psychoactive qualities of the botanical world.”

There is one rather grim twist, however: The spectral cavalcade wasn’t riderless. In fact, the team believes the herd of ghost horses was created to serve a human sacrifice, the cannabis may have been a final send-off. “The likely involvement of human sacrifice leading to the creation of a spectral cavalcade would have potentially made the plant a useful agent to calm individuals who were to be included in the rituals,” the researchers wrote.

It provides a whole new meaning of being stoned to death.

title: Inside King Tutankhamun’s Tomb, 104 Years After Its Discovery - Nautilus
content:
The discovery of King Tutankhamun’s tomb in the Valley of the Kings started with the top of a staircase. On November 4, 1922, archaeologists led by Englishman Howard Carter cleared away rubble that had built up some 3,000 years prior. They were digging for the tomb of Ramesses VI. What they found was a step leading downward.

This wasn’t a pioneering expedition into unknown territory. The Valley of the Kings had been extensively studied and excavated before, but Tutankhamun’s tomb had remained hidden—and relatively well protected from looters.

In effect, the work done on one ancient pharaoh’s tomb (Ramesses VI) had helped preserve Tutankhamun right next door. In the intervening millennia, no one had cleared away these limestone chippings, and it wasn’t widely believed that there was another tomb to be found on the site. But once Carter’s team found the staircase, they made rapid progress. A sealed door at the bottom of the stairs displayed Tutankhamun’s name. Beyond that, there was a passage of rubble and a second sealed doorway.

The tomb was finally breached on November 26th, through a small hole Carter made to push a candle through and assess what was inside. “As soon as one’s eyes became accustomed to the glimmer of light, the interior of the chamber gradually loomed before one, with its strange and wonderful medley of extraordinary and beautiful objects heaped upon one another,” Carter wrote in his journal.

The actual burial chamber—and Tutankhamun in all his regal glory—wouldn’t be discovered until February 16th, as the archaeologists went deeper into the tomb. But it was immediately apparent that this was the most complete and undisturbed Egyptian tomb discovered in modern times—offering up an unprecedented collection of ancient artifacts. More than 5,000 objects in all were removed for museum display, including the golden burial mask, coffins, furniture, clothing, jewelry, weapons, and chariots.

Tutankhamun’s tomb was far from the biggest or grandest to be discovered by archaeologists, but what made it special was how undisturbed it was, adding finer detail to what was already understood about pharaohs and their burial customs.

If you find yourself in the Valley of Kings today, you can still visit the king in his final resting place—walking down the same steps Howard Carter did more than a century ago.

title: The Year Math Changed Forever
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
There is an explanatory elegance to Rivka Galchen’s writing for The New Yorker that I’ve admired for a long time. Here, it finds a superb partner in the mind of Terence Tao, a renowned mathematician. As artificial intelligence casually spits out answers to notably evasive problems, Tao and his colleagues wrestle with the existential implications for their field. Galchen’s profile of Tao is also a demonstration of mathematics as human lineage and artistic practice, a chain of problems that has long encouraged expansive thinking. That chain now appears strained to the point of breaking—a potential “decoupling,” Galchen writes, of “problem-solving and insight.” Don’t miss the superb ending on this one.

“Let me be clear. There was no fun in this for me,” he said. “The fun was had before I gave it to this computer program. But talking to the A.I. about it—this is not fun.” He recalled, as a kid, falling in love with logic puzzles. What he loved was being in the dark, trying to find his way forward. “The fun part was not understanding, and struggling to understand,” he said. “Having all the solutions written down is the least fun part.”

More stories from the intersection of problem-solving and insight

What Can We Gain by Losing Infinity?

Gregory Barber | Quanta Magazine | April 29, 2026 | 3,985 words

“Ultrafinitism, a philosophy that rejects the infinite, has long been dismissed as mathematical heresy. But it is also producing new insights in math and beyond.”

Have We Been Measuring Mountains All Wrong?

Gordy Megroz | National Geographic | September 16, 2025 | 2,432 words

“A new method for quantifying grandeur is reshuffling the pecking order of the planet’s most impressive peaks. Turns out Everest has steep competition.”

At 17, Hannah Cairo Solved a Major Math Mystery

Kevin Hartnett | Quanta Magazine | August 1, 2025 | 2,227 words

“After finding the homeschooling life confining, the teen petitioned her way into a graduate class at Berkeley, where she ended up disproving a 40-year-old conjecture.”

title: “Club Kid” Is a Disarming Cocktail of Grit and Fantasy
author: @NewYorker
content:
Early on in “Club Kid,” an exuberantly entertaining comedy from the writer and director Jordan Firstman, an Uber pulls up outside a Manhattan night club and, like an app-summoned clown car, disgorges an unruly load of human cargo. There’s Peter Green (Firstman), a scruffy, dark-haired man in his twenties; his flinty-eyed business partner, Sophie (Cara Delevingne); and several other friends, all of them pumped to drink, dance, and do ketamine bumps into the wee hours. Peter and Sophie work as party promoters within the city’s queer-club scene, tasked with scheduling events, booking d.j.s, and overseeing guest lists. As they stride up to the venue, the camera sweeping alongside them, Peter sets to work; he sizes up the long line, pulls in someone he recognizes, and then loses himself in the crowd. Watching him work the room, chat with other partygoers, and dance up a storm, you get the sense of a guy who mixes business and pleasure in unsustainable proportions—and who looks out for others better, perhaps, than he looks out for himself.

“Club Kid” is Firstman’s filmmaking début, and he proves as skilled a ringmaster behind the camera as Peter is inside a night club. The movie exudes a startling confidence, at once buoyant and grounded—the kind of assurance that can emerge when a young director’s grasp of the medium, however nascent, is in synch with his feel for his characters and their world. The film’s giddy opening moments fall into a tradition of New York movies that sweep us up, in a disorienting, intoxicating blur, into the city’s after-hours enclaves. Following Peter through this strobe-lit hothouse, you might flash back to “Anora” (2024), which laid bare the fleshy delights of a strip club with a mercantile matter-of-factness. (The two films share a producer, Alex Coco.) All the scenes at Peter’s parties have a touch of an underground sociology lesson. The uninitiated in the audience will learn a thing or two about which drugs to take and not to take, and they may also pick up some irreverent, up-to-the-minute slang: a cocaine-ketamine cocktail is described, at one point, as “a little Charlie, a little Kirk.” Through it all, Peter looks after the guests, most of them gay men and trans women, with a disarming show-you-a-good-time assurance. He isn’t above having a good time himself, even when it pushes against his own boundaries. When Leonora (Paris Petitjean), a British cisgender woman, comes on to him on the dance floor, he tells her that he’s “never touched a vagina in my life.” There’s a first time for everything, and Leonora pulls Peter and another guy into a drug-addled threesome. For Peter, it’s the most random of sex acts, and also the most consequential.

Cut to a decade or so later: Peter returns one day to his apartment, in Brooklyn, and finds a ten-year-old boy named Arlo (Reggie Absolom) waiting for him. Arlo, who has a springy mop of hair and soulful eyes, is the biological son Peter never knew he had. Until recently, the boy was living with his mother, in London. But Leonora has recently died, and apparently Peter is the only person in a position to step up and look after the boy. We hear all this from Leonora’s hard-partying friend Edison (Kirby Howell-Baptiste), rattling off the details with a motormouthed wit that succeeds in selling us on the rather tortured soap-opera plot she’s recapping. Although Peter’s name is on Arlo’s birth certificate, a harder-edged script—or a more cynical protagonist—might have insisted on a paternity test. But “Club Kid” cuts to the quick, with a good-vibes breeziness that, arguably, bespeaks a deeper honesty—a silent contract established with the viewer about the story they’re being told and the pleasures that it will provide. From the moment the kid shows up, there’s little doubt where we’re headed: Arlo is Peter’s, Peter is Arlo’s, and their long-overdue encounter is the film’s raison d’être.

The potential narrative obstacle, then, has less to do with plausibility than predictability. The odd-couple pairing of an adorable moppet and an unlikely guardian, biologically related or not, is among the hoariest of movie formulas, but also the most versatile: sometimes you get “The Game Plan,” a Dwayne Johnson football-and-fatherhood vehicle, from 2007, and sometimes you get a classic like John Cassavetes’s “Gloria,” from 1980. But the specifics of milieu can provide their own novelty, and Firstman’s delirious immersion in queer-club culture proves a threefold triumph—a source of atmosphere, comic mileage, and dramatic tension alike. For Peter, a decade’s worth of semi-lucrative hedonism has taken its toll, and he now stumbles through his days in what feels like a perpetual hangover. His working relationship with Sophie has frayed, money is scarce, and he deals drugs to help cover the rent—the same substances that have battered his mind and body. (“NO MORE DRUGS. THEY DO NOT FEEL GOOD ANYMORE,” he types into his phone after an especially rough night.)

An unexpected shot at fatherhood is both the last thing Peter needs and, in the movie’s unsurprising yet wholly enjoyable formulation, the best thing that’s ever happened to him. Arlo is a living, breathing incentive for Peter to get healthy and sober and figure out, just in time, what to do with his life. It helps that Arlo, winningly played by Absolom, is smart, easygoing, and startlingly well-adjusted for a child who hasn’t enjoyed the stablest of childhoods. Edison mentions an abusive boyfriend of Leonora’s, and there is one scene, set at a public park, where some of Arlo’s suppressed trauma flares violently into the open. Other than that, the most inconvenient thing about him is a dairy allergy. What he’s absorbed from Leonora is a passion for music and a preternatural ease around the club scene that, in every sense, spawned him. No wonder Peter, cash-strapped as he is, can’t resist spending three hundred bucks on an Elliott Smith vinyl record that catches his son’s eye. And no wonder Arlo clicks so quickly with Saffron, a transgender d.j. who shows him the track-spinning ropes.

Saffron is played by Saturn Risin9, one of several nonprofessional actors, including Alaska Riley, whom Firstman recruited from New York’s L.G.B.T.Q.+ party scene, and who infuses the picture with raucous energy and sustained warmth. Not every character comes fully into focus, but among the most quietly vivid is a guy named Devon (the actor and comedian Nigil Whyte), who can applaud Peter’s embrace of fatherhood one moment and wax poetic about the joys of fisting the next. However unlikely it might seem, Peter has been an intuitive fit for his new role all along. Taking care of others, and fostering family within a community, has always come more naturally to him than he realizes.

Firstman’s first several years in the entertainment industry have been their own journey of loopy self-discovery. After getting his start as a writer on the HBO series “Search Party” and as a director of short films, he became an internet star during the COVID-19 pandemic, when several of his comedy videos went viral. When I attended the Independent Spirit Awards in February, 2020, I had no idea that it was Firstman who had written one of the show’s best bits, a hilarious musical tribute to non-obvious examples of gayness in recent movies. (“The title of the film ‘Diane,’ ” the Gay Men’s Chorus of Los Angeles intoned solemnly, “Octavia Spencer playing a history teacher,” and then crescendoed into a multi-film lovefest for Laura Dern.) Years later, Firstman weighed in more sharply on queer representation when he pointed out that the sex scenes in “Heated Rivalry,” the hit series about closeted hockey players, were “not how gay people fuck.” (Amid considerable backlash, he swiftly apologized for the comment.)

Before “Club Kid,” Firstman’s most prominent film role was in “Rotting in the Sun” (2023), a comic mystery thriller that featured some gleefully unsimulated demonstrations of how gay people fuck. His performance had a cheekily meta streak: he played a social-media-influencer type named Jordan Firstman—a fatuous, often full-frontal narcissist who was revealed, in one of the film’s sweeter, slyer twists, to be a figure of surprising intelligence and loyalty, someone you couldn’t help but root for. My sense at the time was that he had a healthy awareness of the obnoxiousness of his own persona and an impressive ability to manipulate and even subvert it. In “Club Kid,” he has us fully on his side from the start. Peter, for all his poor choices, is never as exasperating as he is likable, and he’s never more likable than when he realizes, with shock, how much Arlo means to him.

The film is a wondrous fusion: comedy blurs almost imperceptibly into drama, and realism becomes almost interchangeable with fantasy. In a moment of pure wish fulfillment—which is to say, a classic rom-com trope—Peter takes Arlo to see a social worker (Diego Calva), who turns out to be the dreamiest love interest imaginable: sensitive, gorgeous, and in desperate need of an education in the films of Gregg Araki. But wish fulfillment has its limits, and the canniness of the movie lies in its precise understanding of when and where those limits fall. When Peter reluctantly allows Arlo to d.j. at a party, it’s both an irresponsible risk and a glorious success—and Firstman, refusing to deny either aspect of the experience, uses it to bring father and son to an inevitable point of crisis. There’s a brief battle for Arlo’s future, conducted without ill motives or rancor from anyone, and blessed with a performance, as Peter’s attorney, by Vicki Pepperdine. Her presence confirms that Firstman has cast the movie with care, down to the smallest roles. The film ends with one last punctuating burst of laughter, with a lingering aftertaste of wistfulness and hope. Every club kid must grow up, Peter very much included. ♦

title: Roy Lichtenstein’s Witty Critiques of Masculinity
author: @NewYorker
content:
“Roy Lichtenstein: Like New” (at the Whitney through May 10th) is a masterpiece of curation and design, an exhibition that positions Lichtenstein as the last happy white man in American art. Organized with esprit and imagination by the artist Alex Da Corte and the curator Meg Onli, it’s the first retrospective of Lichtenstein’s work in New York since his splash at the Guggenheim in 1993. The show takes up the museum’s entire fifth floor and ends as it begins: with the artist’s signature brightly colored brushstrokes, lines, and Benday dots causing pleasurable kinetic movements in the mind. Lichtenstein’s dynamic style is ubiquitous by now—as are his professional sheen and finish—but that doesn’t cancel out his winning charm, which, like most charm, can warm you up or wear you out. At “Like New,” you may experience both feelings. It’s a show that aims to keep the real world, our gothic political climate included, at bay, while also distracting us from what one might call the grief porn of contemporary art and its constant reminders of our failures as humans.

For years now, the Whitney has foregrounded race- and gender-based political art, and it’s a little trippy to walk around this show’s pearl-gray-painted rooms, looking at Lichtenstein’s Fantastik-clean white world of orderly studios, shiny blondes, and square-jawed men, in a place where white male power has been repeatedly denounced and the sins of past neglect redressed. No one can make up for the past—certainly not by demanding that it be corrected in the present—and it was perhaps inevitable that the Whitney would have to turn, or return, to white men with name recognition to get people back into its galleries post-COVID. Exhibitions devoted to Jasper Johns and Andy Warhol helped, and still fit the Whitney framework: both artists were queer. And although Lichtenstein wasn’t gay, there’s enough irony about gender in his early work to qualify him as being interestingly gay-adjacent.

Still, it’s difficult to entirely undo the way we’ve been viewing art for a while now, and, after having a great time at “Like New,” you may find yourself feeling slightly guilty about it. But one of the more poignant subtexts of the show is that it’s a reminder of the New York avant-garde in the sixties, and of what a beautiful, forceful energy there was to its various voices, with Lichtenstein the least dirty and anarchic of them all. There’s a sweetness in that, and a sadness, too.

I first spent time with Lichtenstein’s work in the early eighties, when I took a class at Columbia on the art of the nineteen-sixties. The professor led us from the glory days of Abstract Expressionism in the fifties, through the emergence of Robert Rauschenberg and Johns by the end of that decade, to this new era in American art. Inspired by Marcel Duchamp and his poetry of the everyday, Rauschenberg and Johns used commonplace objects—a flashlight, a bedspread—in their creations. But artists working under the Pop-art banner in the sixties, including Lichtenstein, Claes Oldenburg, James Rosenquist, Tom Wesselmann, Marisol, and Warhol, picked at the surface of the world that had made them, in order to show us how much it could reveal about what lay beneath it. You can still feel, in the memorable work produced during that period, the critical embrace of all those dance-lesson diagrams, Campbell’s soup cans, ice-cream cones, and Coca-Cola bottles, alongside images of electric chairs, car crashes, and atomic-bomb detonations.

In the Cold War universe, where everyone was isolated and class was defined by the power to acquire (and to oppress), Pop artists painted or sculpted what they saw and heard. The artist’s “aura” had no place in those works; instead, Pop art was a kind of supersonic whistle heralding the disasters to come, that had already come. But unlike, for instance, Rosenquist, in such charged political pieces as “F-111” (1964-65), which juxtaposes consumer objects with missiles, Lichtenstein made work that was less about conscience than about control, and the eradication of mess, of feeling.

Lichtenstein became Lichtenstein in 1961, when he made “Look Mickey.” He had flirted with cartoon characters before then, but “Look Mickey” took things further. Four feet by nearly six, the painting features the brightest of reds, blues, and yellows. In it, Mickey Mouse and the bombastic Donald Duck are standing on a dock, fishing. Mickey covers his laughing mouth because Donald thinks he’s hooked a fish, but the hook is caught on his own coat. The delight of the painting is the pleasure that Lichtenstein took in the joke—and in this new way of making work that was both free and not free of the artist’s hand. (In the age of Pop, achieving an automated look was part of the process.)

Decades before Richard Prince made his fantastic and forlorn cartoon paintings, Lichtenstein was already exploring the idea of entertainment and raising questions: If cartoons were a form of entertainment, was painting a cartoon a form of entertainment, too? Was modern art a put-on? Or something that could be put on? One question that the Whitney show didn’t answer for me was how Lichtenstein got to cartoons, and then to his comic-strip paintings, with their speech balloons, women in distress, and silent men—whose reserve makes us wonder if their creator was a silent man, too.

Born in 1923, into an upper-middle-class German Jewish family in New York, Lichtenstein grew up on the Upper West Side, with easy access to museums and other cultural institutions. He loved music and art, and in 1940 he enrolled at Ohio State University, where he studied life drawing, painting, and the work of the masters, including Picasso. If he insisted on pursuing art, his parents felt, it would be good for him to get a degree, in case he had to teach to get by.

The Whitney retrospective includes “Drawing by Seeing,” a short film about Lichtenstein’s artistic education, made by Da Corte, whose own work includes video, performance, and installations, driven by the kind of avant-gardism that Lichtenstein espoused for a time. The film is shot in color, but with the performers and their costumes colored a “Twilight Zone” gray. It features a voice-over drawn from a text by Hoyt L. Sherman, Lichtenstein’s teacher and mentor at Ohio State. Sherman’s work centered on perception; he’d flash an image on a screen and then have his students draw what they had seen. Or hadn’t. Da Corte’s film also animates some of Lichtenstein’s early works, including “Step-on Can with Leg” (1961), a two-panel painting that shows a woman’s high-heeled foot stepping on the pedal of a closed garbage can, and then the same image with the lid open. Like Warhol, in “Before and After,” a study of a nose job, also from 1961, Lichtenstein was interested in how time can be represented in a static medium, thus changing how we see a thing, or making us realize that we weren’t really looking.

Lichtenstein’s studies were interrupted when he was drafted, in 1943, but he returned in 1946 to finish his degree on the G.I. Bill. By 1949, he was married to the artist Isabel Wilson Sarisky, with whom he had two sons. (Divorced in 1965, he married Dorothy Herzka, a philanthropist, in 1968.) Lichtenstein, shy and reclusive, was a responsible fellow; he supported his family by teaching, while making art that was at first representational, then a little abstract, not terribly distinguished. The breakthrough came in 1960, when he was teaching at Douglass College (which later became part of Rutgers), where he met the performance artist Allan Kaprow, who introduced him to Claes Oldenburg and George Segal, artists who were as taken with the look and signs of masculinity as Lichtenstein was. (Oldenburg’s 1959 work “ ‘Empire’ (‘Papa’) Ray Gun,” for instance, plays on the phallic shape of a firearm.) Surely the freedom that Lichtenstein saw in those sculptors’ work and at Kaprow’s “happenings” helped to release him and open him up to his strongest qualities as an artist: his interest in gender and his amused wit.

Lichtenstein’s wonderful early work “Masterpiece” (1962) still makes me laugh. In it, a couple are looking at a canvas. The woman, a blonde, has a speech balloon issuing from her red lips: “Why, Brad darling, this painting is a masterpiece! My, soon you’ll have all of New York clamoring for your work!” The man is silent, only partially visible, in profile; the woman is our focus. She may be the kind of woman who needs her man to be a success, in order to validate her power as a woman, one who, unlike Donald Duck, has caught a big one. It’s a joke on the bright and shiny, profit-driven art world, where nothing resonates like success. Among other great early works, there’s the funny, ’tude-filled “Ohhh . . . Alright . . .” (1964)—a closeup of a red-haired woman on the phone, looking slightly annoyed as she speaks the title—and “Drowning Girl” (1963), in which a blue-haired woman with tears falling from her closed eyes drowns as much in misbegotten love as in a swirl of black-and-white waves. A thought bubble reads, “I don’t care! I’d rather sink—than call Brad for help!”

These are not really paintings about distress or isolation. They’re about fake feelings in a manufactured world. What was real in Pop? What wasn’t? I liked these works so much when I was younger, and still do, because, for me, Lichtenstein was at his strongest when he wasn’t just a straight man but, rather, a Warhol-adjacent straight man who could critique both masculinity and the self-consciously feminine. The truth is that when Lichtenstein stopped painting “gay,” I stopped looking. From the seventies on, in work that seemed influenced by Léger, Matisse, Picasso, and others, he appeared to be more at play with the straight boys than questioning their performative creativity. (The Whitney curators have put some of the gay back into his work by treating it as a kind of exquisite California-modern decoration; all that’s missing are gray throw pillows.) Still, at the end of the show, I stood by Da Corte’s replica of Lichtenstein’s enormous 1967 work “Super Sunset Billboard,” which shows a horizon and, above it, white streams of light shooting up and out, like klieg lights announcing a show. The painting is the show. Da Corte and Onli have placed the piece in front of a wall of windows overlooking the Hudson; it’s a calming, lovely thing to see a “real” sky echoing Lichtenstein’s. It’s also a thrilling and moving coda to his work—so much so that I got goosebumps. It was the first time I’d ever thought of goosebumps as Benday dots. ♦

title: The Overwrought Insistence of “La Bola Negra”
author: @NewYorker
content:
It starts with a bang—a fiery explosion, a cloud of smoke, a horrific bloodbath. The year is 1937, deep into the Spanish Civil War, and a group of villagers have gathered to cheer on the right-wing Nationalists against the left-wing Republicans and to welcome the intervention of Benito Mussolini’s troops. The consequences of their Fascist alignment land with a fuck-around-and-find-out swiftness that would be funny if it weren’t so hellish: just as a band starts to play, Italian planes drop a friendly-fire payload, killing many and sending survivors fleeing in terror. Among them is a wide-eyed young trumpet player who makes a detour through a ruined church, where a large, toppled statue of St. Sebastian blocks his path—a sad sight, but also a happy accident. Grabbing onto the thick arrows protruding from the statue’s chest, he clambers over the wreckage and makes his way to safety.

So begins “La Bola Negra,” an extravagantly overwrought epic from the Spanish directors and screenwriters Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, with the first of a few clever, if tortured, winks. The trumpeter (played by the singer Guitarricadelafuente, in his screen-acting début) is himself named Sebastián, though when he beholds that fallen statue he sees only a means of escape, not a famously martyred namesake or a marble-muscled icon of homoerotic desire. The filmmakers see all, though, and not always to their advantage; they approach their characters with an omniscient loftiness, a big-picture grandiosity that too often crowds the smaller sculptural details out of the frame. “La Bola Negra,” which runs close to three hours and unfolds across nearly a century, wants to be a sweeping historical epic of gay longing—a film about what it means to be a man who desires other men in times of war and peace, and who must either resist or surrender to the fascism of the closet. Upon the ruins of St. Sebastian, Ambrossi and Calvo mean to erect a cinematic monument for the ages; instead, they have produced a film that insists, arrogantly and aggressively, on its own monumentality.

Sebastián’s mother is killed in the attack, a presumably devastating shock that is waved almost impatiently aside. He survives, barely, by joining the Nationalist Army: “I’m one of you,” he promises, and his words hover unsettlingly in the air. There’s a delicacy to Sebastián, a hushed fearfulness, that sets him apart from his new comrades. At a seaside military base, he looks on, with furtive lust, as the other men walk, play, bathe, swim, piss, and practice formations in the nude—a sequence to remind some, fondly, of “Sebastiane” (1976), Derek Jarman and Paul Humfress’s feverishly horny reimagining of the saint’s life and martyrdom. The soldiers here are fine-looking men in service of an ugly cause, and one thing that “La Bola Negra” gets right, and trusts us to grasp on our own, is that beauty draws no moral distinctions. Sebastián’s attention can be readily magnetized by his fellow-Fascists one moment and by a prisoner of war the next, which is exactly what happens. When Rafael Rodríguez Rapún (Miguel Bernardeau), a Republican freedom fighter with piercing eyes and a lower abdominal wound, is wheeled into the infirmary, Sebastián is assigned to watch over him and extract information. Yet Rafael, willing and even eager to die for his antifascist principles, returns Sebastián’s gaze without flinching, and with a sense of rebuke that is complicated by unspoken yet unmistakable flickers of desire.

Sebastián and Rafael are not the only characters of note. Ambrossi and Calvo go by the two-in-one moniker Los Javis, and so it shouldn’t surprise us that they approach their narrative in a similar spirit of multitasking compression. The movie consists of three stories, set in three different time frames, and unfurls them simultaneously, in a hyper-controlled frenzy of crosscutting. Sebastián’s tale, adapted from the play “La Piedra Oscura,” by Alberto Conejero (who is credited as Ambrossi and Calvo’s co-writer), is the most substantial of the three, and the other two stories coil around it tightly, like tensile vines. Not long after meeting Sebastián, we are whisked off to Granada, in 1932, where Carlos (Milo Quifes), a reserved, elegantly dressed young man, applies for membership at an exclusive casino. But the casino committee rejects his bid, owing, we later learn, to cruel yet accurate rumors of his homosexuality: “Bola negra, bola negra, bola negra” goes the refrain, as one damning black ball after another rolls down the pike. Carlos’s rich, image-conscious father orders him to return to the casino the next day and refute the suspicions. His mother, a more quietly supportive soul, encourages him to move to Madrid, where he can live more freely.

We get a bracing taste of that liberation in the third strand: it’s 2017, and Alberto (Carlos González), a Madrid-based historian, need only look to Grindr to satisfy an urge (“Sex now,” he types, before he’s uttered a word). Quite the contrast with Carlos, who must stalk some potential trade through the streets at night, and with Sebastián, whose throat goes dry at the mere sight of Rafael’s bare chest. You could argue that Ambrossi and Calvo are old-school romantics at heart, alive to the teasing thrill of the forbidden, and accordingly skeptical of the modern age and its all too convenient spoils. Alberto himself seems nostalgic for the tensions of a crueller bygone era, if the thesis that he’s writing—it involves queer dissident musicians from the nineteen-twenties—is any indication.

A knottier research project awaits him. Alberto learns that his grandfather—whom his mother, Teresa (Lola Dueñas), was bitterly estranged from and never introduced her son to—has recently died and left him a curious inheritance, a mystery that needs untangling. The answers, the viewer can probably guess, will bring the 1932 and 1937 chapters into unifying focus, and although González makes Alberto an engaging enough sleuth, he can’t transcend the passive, puzzle-solving function that the character has been assigned. In the words of Alberto’s concerned boyfriend (Julio Torres), revealing more about the film’s shortcomings than he perhaps intends, “Isn’t it funny that the only story you don’t care about is your own?”

Before “La Bola Negra” won the Best Director award at this year’s Cannes Film Festival (an honor it shared, hilariously, with Paweł Pawlikowski’s exquisitely minimalist “Fatherland”), Ambrossi and Calvo were known for many things. They were a Spanish-entertainment power couple for more than a decade before ending their relationship late last year. Their past collaborations include several TV series—including the popular “Veneno,” a portrait of the transgender sex worker and entertainer Cristina Ortiz Rodríguez—and a feature film from 2017, “La Llamada,” adapted from their own stage musical. They are also card-carrying cinephiles, as their recent interviews have taken pains to flaunt: “La Bola Negra,” they’ve said, carries the artistic DNA of wartime-youth classics such as Andrei Tarkovsky’s “Ivan’s Childhood” (1963) and Elem Klimov’s “Come and See” (1987), and also Claire Denis’s masterwork of soldier-sublimated eroticism, “Beau Travail” (2000). My own mind drifted toward other great films, including Hou Hsiao-hsien’s “Three Times” (2006), a century-spanning trilogy that at once preserves and subverts the boundaries of linear time, and Terence Davies’s “Benediction” (2022), a wrenching biographical portrait of a war veteran and poet who regards his own same-sex desires with profound ambivalence.

But the queer art-house touchstone I’ve heard referenced most often in connection with “La Bola Negra” is Stephen Daldry’s “The Hours” (2002), a mutually unflattering comparison if ever there was one. In both films, everything comes in threes, the incessant crosscutting is accorded a flashy metaphysical weight, and time itself is manipulated, distorted, and rearranged to the point of meaninglessness. The complexities of human longing across the ages are not explored so much as solved, in the manner of a mathematical proof. But what, exactly, is being proved here? The universality of suffering? The magic of editing? Perhaps it’s simply that the most self-consciously expansive films are so often the most reductive, the most diagrammatic—and, incidentally, the most inclined to take refuge in a great artist’s shadow. “The Hours” framed itself as a morbidly repressed valentine to Virginia Woolf, and “La Bola Negra,” with uncloseted exuberance, hitches itself to the mantle of another queer literary giant, Federico García Lorca. Although Lorca isn’t granted his own narrative, his life and legacy—the passion of his left-wing activism, the subversiveness of his art, and the open secret of his homosexuality—make up the tissue that connects all three of the film’s stories.

History has no need for spoiler warnings, but anyone hoping for an untainted experience of the film—a description that applies to no one who’s read this far—might want to skip over the facts that follow. The first is that Rafael Rodríguez Rapún, the P.O.W. who catches Sebastián’s eye, was a real person: a football player, an actor, and a close friend and eventual lover of Lorca’s. The second is that, in 1936, not long before Lorca was murdered by Nationalist forces, he began writing a play called “La Bola Negra,” the bare bones of which—he got only four pages in—inspire another part of the film. No wonder, then, that the tale of Carlos’s blackballing seems to float in a more poetically diffuse register than the other two, at least until the closing stretch, when it takes a hard detour into uncharted realms of snowily lyrical bombast. The wispiness of the written source can go only so far in justifying the fan-fiction tedium of the onscreen result. By this point, Ambrossi and Calvo aren’t so much paying tribute to Lorca as trying to outdo him.

All three stories, whatever their theatrical provenance or cinematic intent, are marred by the same odd insubstantiality; it’s as if the directors, brandishing a rigid narrative and thematic blueprint, were unable to marshal character, dialogue, and action in service of their overarching designs. The 1937 chapter, intended to serve as the film’s spine, suffers most noticeably as a consequence. It isn’t just that Guitarricadelafuente, called on to embody a blur of moral and sexual confusion, settles for looking straight-up perplexed. Even a seasoned performer might have had trouble pulling off the scene in which Sebastián, unable to bear the troops’ violent attack on Rafael, retreats into a corner with his musical instrument and quite literally trumpets his agony to the skies. That’s “La Bola Negra,” more or less (and mostly less): rote trauma divorced from psychology, flailing gestures divorced from meaning. The sole performer who survives this chapter is Miguel Bernardeau, intensely charismatic as the physically frail but spiritually fortified Rafael. Here, in the film’s most memorably composed image, is a man hovering between life and death, his wounded body bathed in an almost celestial light—another allusion to St. Sebastian, and one that signals a tragedy to come.

The other indelible moments in “La Bola Negra” are isolated affairs—focussed, pointedly, on three women on the narrative periphery, whose roles are amplified by strategic, diva-like concentrations of star power. As a cabaret musician who entertains the troops, Penélope Cruz is a wickedly brassy marvel—vamping up a storm one minute, grumbling about her menstrual cycle the next, and eventually coaxing even Sebastián out of his mopey shell. Glenn Close, as a Lorca scholar with an earnest backstory of L.G.B.T.Q.+ allyship, arrives bearing the script’s best intentions and its dreariest dialogue, and yet she rises, by dint of her ineffable Closeness, above the dross of the writing. And then there is, most powerfully of all, Lola Dueñas, known for her work with the director Pedro Almodóvar (who is credited as an associate producer in “La Bola Negra”). As a most un-saintlike Mother Teresa, Dueñas gives voice to a seething, inconsolable fury, an assertion of pure, ferocious will, that exposes the preciousness of Ambrossi and Calvo’s poetic and structural conceits. This film is no monument; it’s a bust. ♦

title: The Art of Letting Go
author: Krista Stevens
content:
For The American Scholar, Lisa Russ Spaar offers us beautiful litany of loss in all its various shapes and forms. From those we love to objects like keys, from our teeth to our moral compass, Spaar takes a close look at what we go through when we experience loss at various times in our lives, and how losses tend to stack up as we age.

I’ve informally polled several friends, colleagues, and family members about their first remembered losses. For most, it was when a milk tooth fell out, usually around the age of six. (Surely there are primal reasons many of us dream throughout our lifetimes about our teeth, as important as they are to speaking, eating.) More than 20 years ago, one of my talented undergraduates, Molly, wrote a poem about losing her first tooth while sledding in winter. Upon tonguing the little bloody socket that remained, she wrote, “I taste my death.” That line has haunted me over the decades. Again, our bodies: made for loss. Language: our ability to articulate what that might mean.

I often wonder what was happening in my late mother’s mind as she sank, over a period of 10-plus years, into the tangled ambages of dementia. She lost the names of things and people. She lost any memory of who we were, those of us who cared for her, even her devoted husband, my father. She finally even forgot that she was not only an alcoholic with a fifth of Scotch hidden in the breadbox but also a chain smoker, though she’d occasionally hold a drinking straw to her lips and take a long, deep drag.
